bipartite.note: The translator preserves the basic logic — the arm-pillow encounter is likened to the brevity of a spring-night's dream, and this leads into anxiety about rumor/reputation — but restructures it as a conditional ('Had I made...what had rumour said?') rather than the flat declarative-then-pivot structure of the original, turning the pivot on かひなく into a rhetorical question ('what had rumour said?') before the reputation-fear proper. The two-part logic (trivial encounter vs. weighty consequence) survives, but the mechanics are loosened into a hypothetical narrative frame, weakening the tight enactment of the kakekotoba bridge.

kakekotoba.note: The translator conveys the 'in vain/futile speculation' sense through the rhetorical question about rumour, but the embedded image of the arm (かひな) is not echoed at all in this line — the arm appears only earlier in L1 ('proffer'd arm'), disconnected from the pivot moment, so the pun's simultaneous double-image is lost; only the abstract 'futile reputation-risk' notion survives, and even that is paraphrased rather than pinpointed in a single word.

The rising/spreading of reputation is rendered literally as fame being affected, matching the primary sense of 立つ as applied to 名; no secondary pivot was asserted by the source analysis for this word so this is a straightforward literal rendering.

kigo.note: The translator names the season directly by retaining 'spring-night's dream' as a fixed phrase, preserving both the explicit seasonal word and its traditional association with brevity/insubstantiality, closely mirroring the source's jokotoba function even though it is compressed into a single line rather than spread across three ku.

line_mapping.structural_note: The translator reorders content: the arm-pillow image (originally ku3, following the jokotoba of ku1-2) is placed first, then the spring-night-dream brevity comparison (ku1-2) follows as a qualifying clause, inverting the original's sequence where the seasonal simile precedes the arm-pillow image; the whole first four lines are cast as a conditional 'had I...' construction not present grammatically in the source.

Dickens.translator_strategy: Dickens recasts the poem as an English conditional lyric with rhyme and meter, prioritizing narrative clarity and euphonic verse form over reproducing the precise mechanics of the jokotoba-kakekotoba pivot.

bipartite.note: The translation keeps the general logic of a brief, dream-like encounter (kami) followed by anxiety over a resulting rumor (shimo), but the boundary is blurred: 'what a shame' (line 3) begins the shimo-ku emotional content while still finishing the kami-ku image of the arm-pillow, so the two halves bleed into one continuous sentence rather than standing as a clear simile-then-consequence structure.
bipartite.relationship_type: simile-implicit collapsed into a single run-on exclamation

kakekotoba_handling.note: The translator conveys only the abstract regret ('what a shame') and drops both the literal 'in vain' sense and the embedded pun on かひな (arm); the physical arm image from 'Thy arm for my pillow' is present but not linked wordplay-wise to the regret expressed afterward, so the pivot's double meaning is lost entirely.
The translator renders the conventional 'a rumor will arise' sense directly and does not attempt any secondary pivot, consistent with the source analysis noting this is not a strong true kakekotoba.

kigo_handling.note: The translator names the season directly with 'Spring night dream,' preserving the explicit seasonal word and its association with brevity and dreaminess, though the atmospheric fragility is compressed into a short simile rather than elaborated.

Noguchi.translator_strategy: Noguchi prioritizes compact lyrical exclamation over preserving the pivot wordplay, rendering the poem as a single flowing sigh of regret rather than reproducing the structural pause between the dream-image and the anxiety about reputation.

entries.content_summary: Emphasizes brevity ('For a short while,—short') corresponding to the fleeting quality of 春の夜

Introduces the arm-pillow (手枕) and pivots into the exclamation of shame/regret (かひなく...惜しけれ, partially)
Completes the fear that a bad rumor will arise (立たむ名こそ惜しけれ)

line_mapping.structural_note: The translation compresses five ku into four lines with line 3 bridging kami and shimo content, splitting the かひなく pivot's dual function across lines 3 and 4 rather than concentrating it in one word, which dissolves the ku-boundary that the pivot originally straddled.

bipartite.note: Porter keeps the structural logic of a brief, dream-like arm-pillow moment (kami) followed by anxiety over reputation (shimo), but compresses the shimo section drastically into a single rhetorical question ('What would the world have said?'), losing the explicit weighing of regret (惜しけれ) and the pivot's wit; the kami/shimo boundary survives but the shimo is thin and generalized rather than a pointed statement about a lasting rumor.

kakekotoba_handling.note: Porter renders the arm image early (L1, 'proffered arm') separately from the 'in vain' sense, which is dropped entirely — there is no word conveying futility or worthlessness of reputation; the pivot's dual meaning is dissolved into a straightforward arm-pillow image and a generic worry, so neither the literal 'in vain' nor the wordplay linking arm/futility survives.

The notion of a rumor or reputation 'arising' is rendered as 'what would the world have said', preserving the primary sense of gossip/reputation spreading, though flattened into a rhetorical question rather than a statement of fear.

kigo_handling.note: Porter explicitly changes the season from spring to summer ('A summer's dream had fled'), replacing 春の夜 with a different named season entirely — this substitutes the source's characteristic fleeting spring-night atmosphere with an unrelated seasonal marker, likely for rhyme with 'fled', losing the connotation of springtime brevity and romantic hazy tone associated with 春の夜 in the waka tradition.

Porter.structural_note: Porter reorders and compresses: the jokotoba (ku1-3) is spread across four lines with the arm-pillow image moved to the front and the dream/season image pushed later, while the entire shimo (ku4-5, containing the pivot and the regret) is collapsed into one closing rhetorical question, losing the かひなく wordplay and the explicit 惜しけれ sentiment.
Porter.translator_strategy: Porter prioritizes a smooth, rhyming English quatrain-plus-refrain over preserving the pivot wordplay and precise seasonal reference, sacrificing かひなく's double meaning and swapping 'spring' for 'summer' to serve rhyme and meter.

bipartite.note: The translation preserves the conditional structure (If... then...) linking the fleeting spring-night dream/arm-pillow to the fear of consequence, but it compresses and slightly flattens the simile into a straightforward conditional clause rather than the more elaborate jokotoba build-up; the logical connection (trivial encounter -> feared reputation) survives but the ku-by-ku richness (esp. the かひな/かひなく pivot) is lost, weakening the structural nuance.

kakekotoba_handling.note: The translator renders かひなく as 'blameless stained' (an odd phrase meaning wrongly/undeservedly stained), capturing only the abstract 'in vain/undeservedly' sense tied to reputation; the embedded かひな (arm) pun is entirely lost, though 'arm' does appear separately in line 3 as 'Pillowed on this arm' — but there is no lexical link between that 'arm' and the 'blameless stained' phrase, so the pivot's wit (arm <-> in-vain) is not reconstructed in English.

The verb 立つ (a reputation 'arising') is rendered through 'my name were... stained', capturing the sense of a reputation coming into being/spreading, though the dynamic verb is replaced by a passive stative construction; no secondary pivot is asserted in the source analysis for this word, so this is treated as a single-meaning rendering.

kigo_handling.note: The translator explicitly names the season ('spring's short night'), directly preserving both the seasonal word and its connotation of brevity/insubstantiality, closely matching the source's 春の夜 imagery of a fleeting, dream-like spring night.

line_mapping.structural_note: The translation follows the ku order closely in a 5-line structure that maps almost one-to-one onto the five ku, though lines 1-2 together cover the jokotoba's first two ku (春の夜の / 夢ばかりなる) and line 4 compresses かひなく立たむ名 into a single clause, losing the internal pivot but preserving the overall sequential logic.

McCauley.translator_strategy: McCauley prioritizes a smooth, moralizing English rendering with explicit seasonal naming and a conditional syllogism, sacrificing the かひな/かひなく wordplay for clarity and emotional resonance ('Hard, indeed, would be my fate').
